Trois observateurs de la vie politique n: Three political observers shared their analysis of the Trudeau era through the lens of the fight against systemic racism.
On peut dire que l’année 2025 a commencé: It’s fair to say 2025 started with a bang on the political front, with the announcement of Justin Trudeau’s resignation after nine years at the helm of the federal government. As always in these situations, the media jumped into the exercise of taking stock. At La Converse, we chose to look at the effect of Justin Trudeau’s decisions on racialized and Indigenous communities across the country.
Trois observateurs de la vie politique n: Three political observers shared their analysis of the Trudeau era through the lens of the fight against systemic racism. They also told us about their concerns for the years ahead under a new government.
<strong>L’annonce de la démission de Jus: The announcement of Justin Trudeau’s resignation kicked off the new political year in spectacular fashion. With his back against the wall, the prime minister is ending nine years at the head of the federal government. While some praise his legacy and his commitment to fighting systemic racism, others are less gentle in assessing his record. All of them, however, fear that some social gains could disappear if a Conservative government is elected.
Dès son arrivée au pouvoir en 2015, Just: From the moment he took power in 2015, Justin Trudeau brought a breath of fresh air to the country. Young, dynamic, cool, and championing multiculturalism as a strength, Canada’s 23<sup>rd</sup> prime minister immediately presented himself as an ally of minorities. Nearly a decade later, with just weeks left in his third mandate, it is time to take stock.
Sous le leadership de Justin Trudeau, de: Under Justin Trudeau’s leadership, Canada recorded significant progress in recognizing racial injustices. He was the first to surround himself with a diverse cabinet, including an Indigenous woman as justice minister, Sikh ministers and two ministers with disabilities, and to appoint a cabinet that respected gender parity.
Cependant, l’effet réel de ses décisions: However, the real effect of his decisions on racialized communities – notably Black and Indigenous ones – and on other minority groups has been uneven, producing symbolic successes but also disappointments once some reforms were completed.
Un constat partagé par plusieurs observa: That assessment is shared by several observers and political players interviewed by La Converse, and behind it looms a fear of a social step backward after the progress of recent years. The prospect of a Conservative government led by Pierre Poilievre worries them more than Justin Trudeau’s departure itself.
<strong>La relation tumultueuse de Justi: Justin Trudeau’s Turbulent Relationship with First Nations
Justin Trudeau l’a souvent répété : il a: Justin Trudeau has said it often: he aimed to be the prime minister of reconciliation. His commitment to Indigenous peoples is considered one of the cornerstones of his three mandates. On September 30, 2021, he launched the first National Day for Truth and Reconciliation. Quite a symbol. But while First Nations welcome some of the progress and do not reject this legacy, the disappointment runs deep.
« J’ai été critique de la politique de T: “I’ve been critical of Trudeau’s policy from the start. It’s true, there have been massive changes in legislation, policy and even in the structure of government over the past nine years. And he poured in tens of billions of dollars, which is much more than Stephen Harper did during the 10 years he was prime minister under a Conservative government. But I think he never intended to change things in a concrete way; I think it was rhetoric,” says Russel Diabo, a Mohawk activist and political analyst.
Selon lui, la réputation d’un Trudeau pr: In his view, the reputation of a Trudeau who was close to First Nations and eager to resolve issues like access to drinking water, reparations, inclusion and land claims is overblown. He particularly regrets the rise of the expression “Indigenous peoples,” which he says erases the “differences that exist between First Nations, Métis and Inuit.”
Parmi les griefs de certains membres des: Among the grievances of some members of Indigenous communities is the big promise made by the Liberal leader as soon as he took office: to implement the recommendations of the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, which was launched under the Conservatives. The result: of the 94 calls to action, only 14 have been implemented. What’s more, over a third haven’t even begun to be implemented, when they aren’t simply blocked, according to <l1>Indigenous Watchdog</l1>.
« Je reconnais à Trudeau le mérite d’avo: “I give Trudeau credit for finding more money, but the problem is that it isn’t enough, because we’re talking about the Indian Act, which has been in place for 148 years now, and which has caused dispossession, poverty and underdevelopment on reserves. And Trudeau invested tens of billions in that very same Indian Act system. He didn’t really change it,” Russel Diabo points out.
Indigenous Watchdog souligne un autre en: Indigenous Watchdog points to another unmet commitment: although Ottawa promised in 2019 to invest $2 billion a year to give Indigenous communities educational support comparable to what the provinces have, that goal has not been reached.
Même chose pour la promesse de campagne: The same goes for the Liberal campaign promise to guarantee access to drinking water for Indigenous communities by 2021. According to the Assembly of First Nations (AFN), its members are 90 times more likely than other Canadians to lack access to drinking water. More than 30 long-term water quality advisories have persisted for decades in some communities.
En 2019, la démission de la première min: In 2019, the resignation of the first Indigenous justice minister, Jody Wilson-Raybould, following pressure from the Trudeau cabinet in the SNC-Lavalin bribery affair, also left a mark. So did the RCMP’s violent crackdown on the Wet’suwet’en, who were opposing the route of the Coastal GasLink pipeline in British Columbia.
Autant d’exemples – et la liste n’est pa: These are just some of the examples – and the list is not exhaustive – that leave a bitter taste for some First Nations, who feel their rights come second to Canada’s economic or political interests. “What Trudeau has been doing for nine years, he does as part of a communications strategy, talking about reconciliation and nation-to-nation relationships. They did everything while saying they were adopting and implementing the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, but in reality they replaced it with a national interpretation. The UN Declaration contains minimum international standards in its articles, but those have been replaced with others that are less beneficial, in Canada,” explains Russel Diabo.
Une autre frange des communautés autocht: Another segment of Indigenous communities, however, places more value on Justin Trudeau’s legacy. All the more so because the context of political uncertainty ahead worries many analysts, including Russel Diabo: “I think the next government will be a majority Conservative government, and I think it will be worse for Indigenous peoples and First Nations.”
Parmi les communautés qui sont les plus: Among the communities most affected by discrimination and police violence in Canada, the Black community benefited from the prime minister’s support on several occasions. Notably, people will remember his participation in the rally against police violence in Ottawa following the murder of George Floyd. The head of government did not hesitate to take a knee for several minutes as a sign of support, despite criticism from some political opponents.
Pour Tamara Thermitus, avocate émérite e: For Tamara Thermitus, an advocate emerita and speaker specializing in discrimination issues, Justin Trudeau’s record is mixed. It must be said that the prime minister has an unflattering past. In 2019, he admitted to having darkened his face black or brown on several occasions at costume events.
« On ne peut pas nier ce que le premier: “You can’t deny what Prime Minister Trudeau has done. He acknowledged his mistakes regarding blackface, that’s one thing; but he also took certain measures, whereas often there are apologies but no action,” says the woman who was the first Black woman to chair the Commission des droits de la personne et des droits de la jeunesse.
M<sup>me</sup> Thermitus souligne notamm: M<sup>s</sup>. Thermitus notes progress in the judicial sphere in particular: “Important work was done to take into account the discrimination Black people experienced in the justice system. But the record is complex, because in concrete terms, you could point out that more minority judges have been appointed, for example, but that’s not an answer in itself. Minority judges also have to take progressive positions for it to truly be an answer. We’ll know by analyzing their rulings.”
Même constat sur le plan économique. Jus: The same goes for the economic front. Justin Trudeau bet on supporting Black entrepreneurs to reduce discrimination, which is particularly pronounced in access to capital, training, networks and more. Last December, the government approved $189 million in funding to extend the <l1>Black Entrepreneurship Program</l1> for five years.
« Oui, ça prend des investissements. Oui: “Yes, it takes investment. Yes, it takes recognition that there were historical injustices. And yes, money is part of compensating for historical injustices,” says Tamara Thermitus. “But at the same time, let’s not kid ourselves, it takes more. Structures also need to be put in place, because putting millions in the hands of individuals is one thing, but if they’re facing systemic discrimination, their business will have a very hard time surviving. Especially since we’re talking about $189 million over five years. We’d need to know how many people will benefit to determine what that means per entrepreneur.”
En matière de violences policières et de: On police violence and racial profiling, here again, Justin Trudeau showed up. In 2020, he declared that “systemic racism is an issue in all our institutions, including in all our police forces, right across the country.”
Pour autant, les personnes noires, autoc: Even so, Black, Indigenous and Arab people remain targets of discrimination by some police officers, according to the statistics. Despite acknowledging systemic racism and supporting reform of police practices, Justin Trudeau did not manage to have a real impact on the criminal justice system and law enforcement.
Il demeure néanmoins difficile de se réj: It nonetheless remains hard to celebrate the prime minister’s departure, since budgets haven’t been passed, which leaves the next government the possibility of reversing some of the commitments Justin Trudeau made, says Tamara Thermitus. “The Conservative Party, like the Trump administration, talks about wokeism and basically wants to go back to a society with people who are part of the spectacle of power games and those who are pushed to the margins,” fears the first Black woman to earn the title of advocate emerita.
‍<strong>Des avancées fragiles dans la l: ‍Fragile Progress in the Fight Against Islamophobia
Marquée par une montée de l’islamophobie: Marked by a rise in Islamophobia – as well as antisemitism – and several tragedies, the Trudeau decade also saw the appointment of Amira Elghawaby. She is Canada’s first Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia.
Un symbole fort pour les communautés mus: A strong symbol for the country’s Muslim communities. In 2019, the prime minister had appointed Irwin Cotler, a former justice minister and attorney general, as Canada’s Special Envoy on Preserving Holocaust Remembrance and Combatting Antisemitism. “Even internationally, it was seen as a very important step forward in recognizing this form of hatred. It was an extremely important step forward, and the work we were able to do was useful, beyond the symbol,” says M<sup>s</sup>. Elghawaby.
Il faut dire que la situation était préo: It must be said that the situation was worrying. In Motion 103, members of the House of Commons asked the federal government to condemn Islamophobia in Canada. The initiative sparked a series of protests and counter-protests across the country. “A few years ago, using the term ‘Islamophobia’ was extremely controversial and politicized. Motion 103, introduced in Parliament, provoked gatherings across the country marked by anti-Muslim hatred,” recalls Amira Elghawaby.
« Nous savons que cette conversation a é: “We know this conversation has been very difficult in Canada, but it has been so crucial.” Not inclined to offer a critical judgment of the policy of the man who created her position, she points out that her office was not the prime minister’s idea. It in fact stems from the 100 recommendations the community made to the federal government following the National Summit on Islamophobia in 2021.
Une année marquée par l’attentat terrori: A year marked by the terrorist attack on the London Muslim Mosque and the deaths of four members of the Canadian Muslim community, a few years after the Quebec City attack. Recall that on January 29, 2017, six people were killed and several seriously injured in a terrorist shooting at the Islamic Cultural Centre of Quebec City. That is why the Trudeau government proclaimed January 29 the National Day of Remembrance of the Quebec City Mosque Attack and Action against Islamophobia.
« Le Canada a connu plus d’attaques isla: “Canada had more deadly Islamophobic attacks against Muslims than any other G7 country from 2017 to 2021. All of this created an environment in which Canadian Muslims felt extremely worried about their safety and that of their families. It was extremely important for the federal government, including the prime minister, to acknowledge how devastating and deadly the phenomenon of Islamophobia had become in our country,” says the former journalist.
Depuis sa nomination, Amira Elghawaby co: Since her appointment, Amira Elghawaby has advised government officials and ministers. “Of course, I spoke with Prime Minister Trudeau several times during my mandate, including very recently, in November, when he committed the government to defining anti-Palestinian racism, which was truly an important recognition of this intersectional form of Islamophobia that affects communities,” says the woman who works independently of the government.
Une question d’autant plus importante qu: An issue all the more important because, over the past year, Justin Trudeau’s image among the Muslim community has deteriorated. At the heart of this loss of trust is Canada’s position on the war Israel has been waging since October 7, 2023.
« Au cours de l’année et demie écoulée,: “Over the past year and a half, Muslim communities have expressed their expectations about what Canada should do in response to the war and violence in Gaza. And there is a lot of disappointment with the federal government’s position,” notes Canada’s special representative. “My mandate is national, but I have spoken about the effects on our local communities. The war in Gaza and the horrific loss of human life there have had an enormous impact on Palestinian Canadians.”
Alors que certaines personnalités contin: While some public figures continue to call for Amira Elghawaby’s resignation, criticizing her for past positions, the possible election of a Conservative government hangs a sword of Damocles over her head and, by extension, over the Muslim community whose rights she defends. Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre has indeed made it clear that he would like her position abolished.
L’avenir des personnes racisées au Canad: The future of racialized people in Canada after Justin Trudeau’s resignation will therefore depend largely on who succeeds him. For even though the various communities give the Trudeau years a mixed assessment, they credit him with a certain goodwill that made dialogue easier, despite disagreements.
<strong>Racisme systémique : 15 moments: Systemic Racism: 15 Key Moments of the Trudeau Decade
<strong>2015 :</strong> Justin Trudeau s: 2015: Justin Trudeau commits to welcoming 25,000 Syrians as civil war rages in Syria. By 2017, Canada will have taken in nearly 54,000 Syrian refugees.
<strong>2017 :</strong> Justin Trudeau c: 2017: Justin Trudeau celebrates diversity in a speech given for Canada’s 150th anniversary. In it he also acknowledges “the mistakes of the past” toward Indigenous peoples, who “have endured oppression for centuries,” and the need for reconciliation.
<strong>2018 :</strong> À l’occasion de: 2018: On Roma Genocide Remembrance Day, the Government of Canada recognizes the Porrajmos (genocide) of the Roma, committed during the Second World War, after decades of requests from Canada’s Roma community. More than 500,000 Roma were persecuted and murdered by the German Nazis and their collaborators.
<strong>2019 :</strong> Le gouvernement: 2019: The Trudeau government allocates $100 million to Canada’s first anti-racism strategy, titled “Building a Foundation for Change: Canada’s Anti-Racism Strategy 2019–2022.” The initiative was renewed for 2022-2024, then for 2024-2028.
<strong>2019 :</strong> Justin Trudeau s: 2019: Justin Trudeau speaks out against Quebec’s adoption of the Act respecting the laicity of the State, or Bill 21. It bans teachers and state officials in positions of authority (police officers, judges, prosecutors, etc.) from wearing religious symbols. After the Court of Appeal’s decision to uphold Bill 21 in February 2024, the prime minister announces that the federal government will intervene if the Supreme Court grants the request of the English Montreal School Board (EMSB).
<strong>2020 :</strong> Le premier minis: 2020: The prime minister appoints Irwin Cotler, a former justice minister and attorney general, as Canada’s Special Envoy on Preserving Holocaust Remembrance and Combatting Antisemitism.
<strong>2020 :</strong> Justin Trudeau s: 2020: Justin Trudeau declares himself in favour of mandatory body-worn cameras for police officers in Canada to fight systemic racism and racial profiling. <strong>2021 :</strong> Création de la J: 2021: Creation of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on September 30 to commemorate the suffering endured by Indigenous peoples.
<strong>2023 :</strong> Justin Trudeau n: 2023: Justin Trudeau appoints Amira Elghawaby as Canada’s Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia. The position did not previously exist.
